Sigma Labs System The Sigma Labs PrintRite3D system, procured in FY2023, has remained dormant at the EI for an extended period. Unfortunately, Sigma Labs ceased operations, leaving the team without a viable option for installation. Undeterred, the team has been actively engaging with former UNCLASSIFIED AMMT – 316H SS Los Alamos National Laboratory Page 3-29 Sigma Labs employees to secure the services of a field engineer capable of setting up the system. After persistent efforts, an ex-field engineer agreed to assist and visited the site on September 16th, 2024. With this crucial step forward, the installation of the PrintRite3D system is now scheduled to take place in mid-October, finally bringing this advanced technology online and unlocking its potential for the team. M290 Cover and Laser Safety Concerns A significant milestone was achieved with the successful mounting of the new 24 MP visible wavelength sensor, replacing its 4 MP predecessor. However, the modified mounting piece, designed to accommodate the camera and cable, inadvertently created a large gap that exposed laser light from the chamber. This setup rendered operation with the machine cover down impossible, prompting a work pause to reassess laser safety aspects. A thorough evaluation revealed that the sensor's mounting position was surrounded by hot glass, spanning wavelengths of [around 1070 nm +/- 10nm], and that the chamber constituted a primary enclosure. Fortunately, it was deemed safe to operate with the cover up, but concerns lingered regarding the lack of a secondary enclosure. To address this, a cover mount was carefully designed and implemented, striking a delicate balance between safety and functionality. Figure 28:Visible Wavelength Sensor Housing. The custom-designed sensor housing, showcased in Figure 28, served a dual purpose: providing a secondary laser enclosure and enabling active cooling. The visible wavelength camera, capable of capturing images at an impressive 18 frames per second with a 24 MP resolution, generated a substantial heat load during operation. To mitigate this, an active cooling scheme was implemented by integrating a compressed air line (red) into the sensor housing. UNCLASSIFIED AMMT – 316H SS Los Alamos National Laboratory Page 3-30 The compressed air flowed over the sensor, maintaining an optimal operating temperature of 50°C. However, the cooling scheme was not without its challenges. The compressed air used to cool the sensor also fed into the machine, resulting in a reduced flow rate and causing the system to struggle to maintain nominal operating pressure. This led to several build pauses, disrupting the operation. Furthermore, the compressor introduced water vapor into the compressed air lines, which became a significant issue when the system required continuous operation to cool the camera.
